title: Root Filesystem
what: The top-level starting point of everything in Linux.
why: Linux mounts all filesystems into a single tree under '/'.
difference: Not the same as /root (root user's home).
modern: Still the canonical hierarchy, with many distros using merged-/usr layouts.

title: Essential User Binaries
what: Critical user commands such as ls, cp, and mv.
why: Core commands must work even in minimal boot/rescue contexts.
difference: Compared with /sbin, /bin is traditionally user-oriented.
modern: Often symlinked to /usr/bin.

title: Boot Loader Files
what: Kernel, initramfs, and bootloader artifacts.
why: Boot components are needed before full userspace starts.
difference: Unlike /usr, this is strictly startup-focused.
modern: UEFI systems commonly also use /boot/efi.

title: Device Files
what: Special files exposing hardware and virtual devices.
why: Linux treats devices as files for consistent access.
deleteImpact: Device communication breaks and system stability drops.
difference: Not regular persisted data like /var.
modern: Mostly managed dynamically by udev/devtmpfs.

title: System Configuration
what: Machine-specific configuration files.
why: Keeps system settings separate from binaries.
difference: Unlike /usr, /etc is local config, not packaged app files.
modern: Still central, with systemd and service overrides heavily using /etc.

title: User Home Directories
what: Default personal directories for non-root users.
why: Separates user data from system internals.
deleteImpact: Users lose personal files and preferences.
difference: Unlike /root, this is for regular accounts.
modern: Desktop app settings are often in ~/.config and ~/.local.

title: Essential Shared Libraries
what: Core shared libraries and kernel modules.
why: Programs need these runtime dependencies.
difference: Compared with /usr/lib, /lib traditionally contains boot-critical libs.
modern: Often merged or symlinked into /usr/lib on many distros.

title: 32-bit Libraries
what: Compatibility libraries for 32-bit binaries on 64-bit systems.
why: Allows legacy or proprietary 32-bit apps to run.
difference: Unlike /lib64, this is for 32-bit ABI.
modern: Present mainly on multilib-enabled systems.

title: 64-bit Libraries
what: Loader and libraries for 64-bit binaries.
why: Defines runtime location for 64-bit architecture libs.
difference: Unlike /lib32, this is for 64-bit ABI.
modern: Often symlink-based in merged library layouts.

title: x32 ABI Libraries
what: Libraries for x32 ABI (rare hybrid ABI on x86_64).
why: Supports specific optimized builds using x32 ABI.
difference: Unlike /lib32 and /lib64, this targets x32 ABI specifically.
modern: Rarely used on mainstream desktop/server installs.

title: Removable Media Mounts
what: Mount points for USB drives and removable media.
why: Provides standardized per-device mount directories.
difference: Unlike /mnt, this is usually auto-managed by desktop tools.
modern: Desktop environments commonly mount user devices here.

title: Temporary Manual Mounts
what: Conventional mount point for temporary manual mounts.
why: Admins need a neutral place for ad-hoc mounting.
difference: Unlike /media, /mnt is usually admin/manual.
modern: Still common for quick maintenance operations.

title: Optional Third-party Software
what: Add-on or vendor-packaged software outside distro defaults.
why: Keeps self-contained applications isolated.
difference: Unlike /usr, /opt often hosts vendor-managed bundles.
modern: Still common in enterprise software deployments.

title: Kernel and Process Virtual Files
what: Virtual in-memory files exposing process and kernel state.
why: Tools inspect system internals through file-like interfaces.
deleteImpact: Cannot be deleted normally; breaking mount hurts observability.
difference: Unlike /var, this is generated at runtime, not on disk.
modern: Still foundational for system inspection tools.

title: Root User Home
what: Home directory of the root user.
why: Ensures root has a home even if /home is unavailable.
deleteImpact: Root user preferences, scripts, and keys can be lost.
difference: Not the same as '/' filesystem root.
modern: Unchanged across major Linux distributions.

title: Runtime Volatile State
what: Volatile runtime data like PID files and sockets.
why: Services need writable boot-time runtime state storage.
deleteImpact: Many services lose runtime state and may fail.
difference: Unlike /var/run legacy path, /run is primary modern location.
modern: Typically mounted as tmpfs and recreated each boot.

title: Essential System Binaries
what: Low-level binaries mainly for administration and repair.
why: Boot and system maintenance require privileged tools.
deleteImpact: Repair and networking administration tools fail.
difference: Compared with /bin, more admin-oriented commands.
modern: Often symlinked to /usr/sbin.

title: Service Data
what: Site-specific data served by system services.
why: Keeps service payload data in predictable location.
difference: Unlike /var, /srv is specifically service-exposed data.
modern: Less universally used, but still valid by FHS.

title: Kernel Device and System Interface
what: Virtual filesystem exposing kernel objects and device attributes.
why: Provides structured interface to kernel and hardware state.
deleteImpact: Cannot be safely removed; system introspection/control breaks.
difference: Unlike /proc, /sys is object-centric device/kernel model.
modern: Core interface for udev and hardware management.

title: Temporary Files
what: Short-lived temporary storage for apps and scripts.
why: Provides shared writable scratch space.
deleteImpact: Running apps may crash if active temp files are removed.
difference: Unlike /var/tmp, /tmp is often cleaned at reboot.
modern: Commonly mounted as memory-backed tmpfs.

title: Userland Programs and Data
what: Most user-space applications, libraries, docs, and shared assets.
why: Organizes non-boot-critical software in a stable hierarchy.
deleteImpact: Most software disappears; system becomes minimally usable.
difference: Unlike /etc, /usr mostly holds package-managed files.
modern: Merged-/usr now consolidates several traditional top-level paths.

title: Variable Runtime Data
what: Frequently changing data: logs, caches, spool, and state.
why: Separates mutable operational data from static binaries.
deleteImpact: Logs, caches, package/service state can be lost.
difference: Unlike /tmp, /var is generally persistent across reboots.
modern: Often placed on separate storage due to heavy growth.

title: Recovered Filesystem Fragments
what: Directory used by fsck for recovered orphaned filesystem data.
why: Filesystem checks need a place to attach recovered inodes.
deleteImpact: You may lose chance to inspect recovered fragments.
difference: Unlike normal directories, this is maintenance/recovery-oriented.
modern: Created on many ext filesystems; usually empty during normal operation.
